# R8 — Symphony late 9:15–10:18 (covenant/death; once-for-all; Ps 40; session; New Covenant re-quote)

**Range read in full:** 3201–3466 (slice `R8_symphony_late_9-10_3201-3466.txt`)  
**Source:** Gareth Lee Cockerill, *The Epistle to the Hebrews* (NICNT, 2012)  
**Evidence class default:** Cockerill (commentator) on Hebrews (primary text under exposition).  
**Structural frame in range:** close of second symphony movement (9:15–22 covenant); third movement 9:23–10:18 (“The New Explained”) — sanctuary 9:23–24; sacrifice 9:25–10:14 (subparts 9:25–10:4 / 10:5–10 / 10:11–14); covenant climax 10:15–18.  
**Suggested page targets:** `hebrews`, `atonement`, `new-covenant`, `priesthood-of-christ`, `gareth-lee-cockerill`, `typology`.

## Claims

### C1 — 9:15: self-offering establishes Christ as New-Covenant Mediator
**Locus:** 3202  
**Quote:** "On account of the effective sacrifice offered by Christ described in v. 14, \"he is\" now \"the Mediator of [the] New Covenant.\" This sacrifice is the death that \"has occurred for redemption of the transgressions based on the First Covenant.\" … By establishing an effective way of approaching God, he terminated the Old Covenant as a way of salvation and inaugurated the New that it typified. His self-offering became a sacrifice of covenant inauguration."  
**Claim:** (Cockerill) On the basis of 9:14’s effective sacrifice, Christ *is* Mediator of the New Covenant; his death redeems transgressions “based on the First Covenant,” ends the Old as a way of salvation, and inaugurates the New it typified—self-offering as covenant-inauguration sacrifice; not mere go-between but guarantor (cf. 7:22) for those who draw near through him (7:25).  
**Pages:** `hebrews`, `new-covenant`, `priesthood-of-christ`, `atonement`, `typology`

### C2 — “Transgressions based on the First Covenant” not limited to pre-Christ offenses
**Locus:** 3204  
**Quote:** "\"Transgressions based on the First Covenant\" does not limit the effectiveness of Christ's sacrifice to offenses committed before his coming or before the hearers became believers. … Apart from Christ the condemnation of the broken covenant described in 8:7-13 continues to threaten the people of God. … Christ's coming has only intensified the condemnation of the Old Covenant on those who reject God's grace (2:1-4)."  
**Claim:** (Cockerill) First-Covenant “transgressions” name the exposed nature of sin as unbelief/disobedience; broken-covenant condemnation still threatens post-Christ people of God; rejection of grace intensifies Old-Covenant condemnation; “transgressions” stresses deliberate seriousness; Christ’s death redeems from consequences *and* power of these transgressions, cleansing so people escape condemnation and receive the inheritance the Old anticipated.  
**Pages:** `hebrews`, `atonement`, `new-covenant`

### C3 — High priesthood and mediatorship as two sides of one ministry
**Locus:** 3206  
**Quote:** "Christ exercises his present ministry both as High Priest at God's right hand and as Mediator of the New Covenant. His high priesthood and his mediatorship are two sides of the same coin. We might say that as High Priest he does what the Old Covenant could not do by cleansing the heart from sin. As Mediator he undoes what the Old did, by removing the condemnation pronounced on the sinner. Yet the two cannot be separated because the New Covenant he mediates results in God's law written on the cleansed hearts of his people (10:15-18). Priesthood and covenant are inseparable (7:11)."  
**Claim:** (Cockerill) Present ministry = High Priest (right hand) + New-Covenant Mediator; High Priest cleanses the heart (what Old could not do); Mediator removes Old’s condemnation; inseparable because mediated New Covenant inscribes law on cleansed hearts (10:15–18).  
**Pages:** `priesthood-of-christ`, `new-covenant`, `atonement`, `hebrews`

### C4 — “Called” → eternal inheritance via Christ’s mediation
**Locus:** 3208  
**Quote:** "\"Those who have been called\" describes God's people in this world. … All who persevere through the mediation of Christ will attain this \"eternal inheritance.\" … Christ has now provided a \"redemption\" that opens the \"eternal inheritance\" in the heavenly homeland (11:10, 13-16) for all the faithful (11:1-40)."  
**Claim:** (Cockerill) “Called” = God’s people under heavenly calling (3:1; Abrahamic promise 11:8); life of faith/obedience; perseverance through Christ’s mediation reaches eternal heavenly inheritance; Exodus pattern (redemption → land inheritance) transposed to Christ-opened eternal homeland; unbelief (3:7–4:11) fails destination.  
**Pages:** `hebrews`, `priesthood-of-christ`, `new-covenant`

### C5 — Structural role of 9:16–22: remove Old-breach condemnation before New blessings
**Locus:** 3214–3216  
**Quote:** "In the covenant section (8:7-13) of the opening movement of this symphony the pastor quoted the New Covenant prophecy from Jer 31:31-34. … In 9:16-22 the pastor shows how Christ removes the condemnation engendered by the Old. In 10:15-18, the final covenant section, he will enumerate the blessings of the promised and now fulfilled New. … Verses 16-17 explain how Christ's sacrifice procured this liberation according to the terms of that First or Old but broken Covenant. Verses 18-22 verify this liberation through a description of the First and Old Covenant's inauguration."  
**Claim:** (Cockerill) Three covenant panels frame the symphony: 8:7–13 (breach + promise); 9:(15)16–22 (removal of condemnation from breach); 10:15–18 (New blessings); 16–17 = how death procures liberation under broken First Covenant; 18–22 = verification via Sinai inauguration blood.  
**Pages:** `hebrews`, `new-covenant`, `atonement`, `gareth-lee-cockerill`

### C6 — Against diathēkē as “will/testament” in 9:16–17
**Locus:** 3218–3220  
**Quote:** "Many English translations use \"testament\" or \"will\" in vv. 16-17, but revert to \"covenant\" in vv. 18-22 … One must question, however, if the pastor would use such wordplay at the expense of the conceptual unity that pervades his sermon. … First, the statement that a \"will\" had no force while its maker was alive does not describe contemporary practice. … Third, \"will\" does not fit what Hebrews says about Christ's death: he does not transfer an inheritance to others by his death. He enters his inheritance, which he then shares with his \"brothers and sisters.\""  
**Claim:** (Cockerill) Rejects testamentary reading of 9:16–17 despite contemporary legal sense of diathēkē: elsewhere Hebrews always means OT covenant; wordplay would sacrifice conceptual unity; contemporary wills could take effect while maker lived; “confirm/force” language suits establishing not executing wills; Christ does not bequeath inheritance by death but enters and shares it; close syntax with 15 and 18–22 forbids meaning-shift.  
**Pages:** `hebrews`, `new-covenant`, `gareth-lee-cockerill`

### C7 — Hahn reading: 9:16–17 concerns *broken* covenant and curse-death
**Locus:** 3224–3228  
**Quote:** "In a truly ground-breaking study Scott Hahn has presented an interpretation that removes this artificiality and shows how \"covenant\" fits admirably in both the immediate and wider contexts. Verses 16-17 are not describing how one establishes a covenant but what must be done when a covenant is broken. … \"For where there is a [broken] covenant, the death of the covenant-maker must be … God's people are the \"covenant-maker\" who broke God's First Covenant. … Until the curse of a covenant falls on the covenant breakers, the validity of the covenant is in question. … \"It is not in force until it is enforced.\""  
**Claim:** (Cockerill, following Hahn) 9:16–17 = death required when covenant is *broken*, not ordinary covenant-ratification; God’s people are covenant-breaker under Sinai pattern; broken covenant “valid” only when curse-deaths fall; v. 17b negative: never in force while covenant-maker lives (enforcement). Rejects both pure “will” and simplistic symbolic self-curse-sacrifice solutions as artificial.  
**Pages:** `hebrews`, `new-covenant`, `atonement`, `gareth-lee-cockerill`

### C8 — “Death of the covenant-maker must be borne”: Christ bears the curse (Isa 53 echo)
**Locus:** 3226  
**Quote:** "He affirms the necessity of the death resultant from the covenant curse, but he does not say by whom it must \"be borne.\" Indeed, the death that has \"occurred\" (v. 15) for redemption from First Covenant violation is the death of the incarnate Son of God that frees the condemned people of God from the covenant curse. He has \"borne\" the death resultant from their sin just as God's Servant in Isa 53:4 \"bore\" the sins of God's people through his suffering. This interpretation is strengthened by the way v. 28 below echoes Isa 53:12 when it says that Christ offered himself once \"to bear the sins of many.\""  
**Claim:** (Cockerill) “Be borne” deliberately leaves agent open: incarnate Son’s death is the death borne for First-Covenant violation; Isa 53:4/12 Servant language; reinforced by 9:28 “bear the sins of many.”  
**Pages:** `hebrews`, `atonement`, `priesthood-of-christ`

### C9 — Sinai inauguration (9:18–22): blood binds under curse; Exodus expanded
**Locus:** 3230–3236  
**Quote:** "According to vv. 18-22 the blood that inaugurated the Old Covenant invoked those consequences upon the sinner. … Hebrews underscores the solemnity of this occasion by adding features from other passages not found in the description of its inauguration according to Exod 24:3-8. … Hebrews says that Moses sprinkled the \"book,\" containing these same stipulations, and the \"people,\" instead of the \"altar\" and the \"people\" as in Exodus. … by this paraphrase he indicates that the blood bound the people, on pain of death, to obey the stipulations proclaimed and now written in the \"book.\""  
**Claim:** (Cockerill) 18–22 confirm 16–17: inaugural blood invoked curse-consequences; Exod 24:3–8 expanded (bulls/goats, water, scarlet wool, hyssop; book not only altar) to stress purification-totality and blood-binding of people to every ordinance under death-penalty; Heb 9:20 paraphrase of Exod (LXX) elevates “This is the blood,” “completed,” final “God.”

### C10 — Possible Last-Supper parallel; Old blood condemns, New blood releases
**Locus:** 3238  
**Quote:** "Moses \"took\" the \"blood\" and \"sprinkled the people, saying, \"this is the blood of the covenant.\" Christ \"took\" the \"cup\" and \"gave it to his disciples, saying, ... for this is my blood of the covenant.\" … Although the hearers may not have been attuned to pick up these clues, it is possible that the pastor used these similarities to suggest a parallel between God's establishing the Old Covenant through Moses and Christ's establishing the New. … The blood of the Old brought condemnation for disobedience; only the blood of the New brought true \"release\" (Heb 9:22)."  
**Claim:** (Cockerill) Cautiously notes Matt 26:27–28 (// Mark) verbal parallels to Moses’ actions/words; may hint Old-inauguration // New-inauguration; structural difference (relative clause on covenant vs. blood); Old blood → condemnation, New blood → true “release.”

### C11 — 9:22: without shedding of blood no release; blood = Christ’s death, release comprehensive
**Locus:** 3240–3246  
**Quote:** "Thus he concludes his evidence for the role of blood in the Old Covenant by saying that \"almost everything\" associated with that Covenant and its Tent \"is purified by blood according to the law\" (v. 22a). … \"without the shedding of blood there is no release\" (cf. Lev 17:11). … The blood that brings this \"release\" can be nothing less than the shed blood of Christ. … The pastor's use is based on the first of these senses, since he employs this term as a powerful description of Christ's death. … The blood of Christ frees God's people from sin, both by cleansing their hearts from its taint and dominion and by releasing them from its condemnation."  
**Claim:** (Cockerill) Pervasive Old blood (tent, utensils; cf. Josephus Ant. 3.206) grounds absolute axiom 9:22; goes beyond “according to the law” and rabbinic blood-necessity talk; “shedding of blood” (from LXX kill/pour language) describes Christ’s death; “release” (aphēsis) without “of sins” is comprehensive—cleansing + liberation from covenant-curse condemnation—not mere forensic forgiveness; stage-setter for 9:23–10:18.  
**Pages:** `hebrews`, `atonement`, `new-covenant`

### C12 — Third movement overview: sanctuary–sacrifice–covenant in major; sacrifice swells
**Locus:** 3252–3266  
**Quote:** "The third movement, 9:23-10:18, brings this grand symphony to its finale. … He plays all three themes — sanctuary, sacrifice, and covenant — in a crescendoing major key. … The theme of sacrifice, so muted in the first movement, swells to overwhelming predominance — three verses in the first movement (8:3-5), five in the second (9:11-15), eighteen (9:25-10:14) in this the third. … At the end of the second movement the pastor anticipated … \"without the shedding of [Christ's] blood there is no release\" (9:22). The corollary at the end of the third … \"where there is release\" provided by Christ \"there is no longer\" need to keep presenting any other \"offering for sin\" (10:18)."  
**Claim:** (Cockerill) 9:23–10:18 = finale of three-movement symphony (8:1–10:18); all themes major; sacrifice section 9:25–10:14 chiastic around 10:5–10 (Ps 40 obedience); 9:23–24 sanctuary seeds 10:11–14; 9:25–10:4 anticipates 10:15–18; frame 9:22 ↔ 10:18 on “release.”

### C13 — 9:23: heavenly things cleansed with better sacrifices (lesser-to-greater typology)
**Locus:** 3270–3280  
**Quote:** "Therefore it was necessary for the pattern of the things in the heavens to be cleansed with these sacrifices, but the heavenly things themselves with better sacrifices than these. … By portraying the old sanctuary … as \"the pattern of the things in the heavens\" he affirms both its inferior status and its typological relationship to the Sanctuary now entered by Christ. … since the \"pattern\" was cleansed by animal sacrifices, then the far greater \"heavenly things\" must be cleansed by proportionately and therefore definitively \"better sacrifices.\" … The pastor uses the plural, \"better sacrifices,\" because he is drawing a parallel with the various sacrifices of the Old Covenant and establishing a general principle before discussing the \"better sacrifice\" of Christ."  
**Claim:** (Cockerill) Mosaic tent = “pattern” (inferior + typological); ultimate sanctuary = “heavenly things themselves”; a fortiori better sacrifices required; plural “sacrifices” = principle/parallel to multi-sacrifice Old system, not denial of once-for-all single sacrifice.  
**Pages:** `hebrews`, `typology`, `atonement`, `priesthood-of-christ`

### C14 — Why heavenly things need cleansing: objective barrier of sin, not Platonic pollution of heaven
**Locus:** 3282  
**Quote:** "Those who contend that Hebrews is dependent on the radical heavenly/earthly dichotomy characteristic of Platonic dualism have the most difficulty explaining how the heavenly world required cleansing. Riggenbach, however, reminds us that it was the sins of the people and not its earthly character that polluted the Mosaic sanctuary. … Lane is correct when he says, \"The writer conceived of defilement as an objective impediment to genuine access to [God].\" Thus by cleansing the heavenly Sanctuary Christ removed this otherwise impregnable barrier and the accompanying threat of judgment. The pastor is not merely repeating what he said about Christ's sacrifice cleansing the \"conscience\" (9:14), and the heavenly Sanctuary is no mere metaphor for human interiority. The sacrifice of Christ has made an \"objective\" difference in the relationship between God and his people."  
**Claim:** (Cockerill) Heavenly cleansing ≠ Platonic dualist problem; sin of the people pollutes access (as Mosaic sanctuary); defilement = objective impediment; Christ removes barrier/threat; not reducible to conscience-cleansing or interior metaphor; objective new fellowship possibility; inaugurates right-hand high-priestly ministry.  
**Pages:** `hebrews`, `atonement`, `priesthood-of-christ`, `gareth-lee-cockerill`, `typology`

**Locus:** 3284–3286

### C16 — 9:25–10:4 structure: once-for-all vs year-after-year; functions and impact
**Locus:** 3296–3300

The first does away with sin (9:26b); the second shows that sin yet continues (10:3). **Claim:** (Cockerill) 9:25–10:4 unified by once-for-all // annual repetition contrast; functions: abolish sin vs memorial of sin; impact: prepares for eternity vs impotence; harvests in 10:15–18 (release / God remembers no more).

### C17 — 9:25–26: not often; absurdity of repeated suffering; once at climax of ages for abolition of sin
**Locus:** 3302–3310

### C18 — Perfect “he has appeared”; future orientation pastoral and theological
**Locus:** 3314–3318  
**Quote:** "With obvious appropriateness and intentionality the pastor has used the perfect tense \"he has appeared\" to affirm the lasting effect of Christ's definitive self-offering accomplished at his first coming. … From a theological perspective, if Christ's saving work was truly the \"climax of the ages,\" then it must also determine the future and the ultimate outcome of history. From the pastoral point of view, focus on the ultimate destiny of God's people is strong motivation for endurance until the end. … The expression \"he has appeared\" also reminds us that, as our High Priest and Savior, Christ fully reveals God and thus accomplishes his vocation as the eternal Son (cf. 1:1-3)."  
**Claim:** (Cockerill) Perfect of first appearing stresses lasting effect; gaze stays on exalted Christ and final destiny; climax-of-ages logically determines future; endurance motivation; appearing = revelatory fulfillment of Son’s vocation; way to God fully disclosed.

### C19 — 9:27–28: human once-death + judgment // Christ once-offered; second appearing salvation without sin-reference
**Locus:** 3320–3326  
**Quote:** "\"it is appointed for human beings to die once for all, and after this, judgment\" … The parallel with Christ's return in v. 28 suggests that the judgment coming \"after\" death is the final Judgment described in 12:26-29. … Christ's second coming to bring final salvation for his people is the ultimate proof that his sacrifice was \"once for all,\" unrepeatable because absolutely sufficient. … \"he will appear a second time without reference to sin for the purpose of bringing salvation to those awaiting him.\" … this phrase echoes what Isa 53:12 says about the Suffering Servant who offers himself for \"the sins of many.\" … by his self-sacrifice Christ took sins as a whole upon himself — not just their deserved punishment. … Just as the high priest returned and blessed the people after offering his sacrifice on the Day of Atonement, so Christ will return with the blessing of ultimate salvation."

### C20 — 10:1: law has only a shadow, not the reality of the good things to come
**Locus:** 3330–3334  
**Quote:** "The last word in the Greek text of 9:28 was \"salvation\"; the first word in 10:1 is \"shadow.\" … \"the law has only a shadow of the good things to come and not the reality itself of those things.\" … The \"law\" is the whole OT system of Tent, priests, sacrifices, purification rituals, and the like, seen as a way of expunging sin and approaching God. … the law was a \"shadow,\" an intimation, a pattern … that made comprehensible the \"reality itself\" yet to come. In fact, the very ineffectiveness of the old system was part of the way in which it exposed human need and pointed forward to the new."  
**Claim:** (Cockerill) Load-bearing OT hermeneutic: law-system as *skia* of coming goods, not *eikōn*/reality itself; shadow includes intentional ineffectiveness as pointer; “good things” = what has come in Christ (9:11) plus final salvation at second coming (9:28).

### C21 — Shadow/reality vs Philo’s Platonic synonymy
**Locus:** 3332  
**Quote:** "The pastor's use of the terms translated \"shadow\" and \"reality\" betrays the distance between his worldview and the Platonic dualism espoused by Philo. Philo uses both words almost synonymously to describe things in the created world as temporal, transitory copies of the eternal world. … The pastor, however, contrasts these two terms. The first is not a somewhat deceptive reflection of the eternal but a divinely ordained, though imperfect, anticipation and foreshadowing of God's full salvation to come. The second is used for the \"reality\" of that salvation itself manifested in Christ."  
**Claim:** (Cockerill) Hebrews’ skia/eikōn contrast is salvation-historical typology, not Philo’s Platonic dualism (where both terms nearly synonymously mark earthly copies of eternal forms).  
**Pages:** `hebrews`, `typology`, `gareth-lee-cockerill`

### C23 — 10:2–3: consciousness vs reminder of sin; memorial of sin year after year
**Locus:** 3340–3342  
**Quote:** "It is tempting to render the word translated \"consciousness\" as \"conscience,\" the meaning it has in 9:14. \"Consciousness,\" however, is the more common meaning and is appropriate by contrast with \"reminder\" in the next verse … Verses 2 and 3 are two sides of the same coin … the perpetual offering of these sacrifices demonstrates their inability to remove sin (v. 2); consequently, they become a continual \"reminder\" that sin still remains (v. 3). … Philo … taught that the offerings of the unjust brought only a reminder of sin because of the character of the person offering. ### C24 — 10:4: impossible for blood of bulls and goats to take away sin
**Locus:** 3344–3346

### C25 — 10:5–10 overview: Ps 40 = incarnate obedience as heart of sacrifice symphony
**Locus:** 3352–3354, 3382  
**Quote:** "These verses contrast the incarnate Son's obedience unto death with the impotent shed blood of animals just mentioned in v. 4. Thus the \"blood\" of Christ is nothing less than his obedient human life offered on the cross. … Psalm 40:6-8 is quoted in 10:5-7 as Christ's affirmation of obedience on the eve of his incarnation. … We conclude, then, that Psalm 40 is the vital link that completes the pastor's argument and integrates his use of these other key OT passages. This OT prophecy reveals the means by which Christ has atoned for sin, entered into his high priesthood at God's right hand, and become Mediator of the New Covenant. Thus it is the heart and unifying center of 8:1-10:18, the symphony in praise of Christ's sacrifice."  
**Claim:** (Cockerill) Christ’s blood = obedient human life offered on the cross; Ps 40:6–8 spoken on eve of incarnation; integrates Jer 31 and Ps 110 trajectories; chiastic center of sacrifice section and unifying heart of 8:1–10:18.

### C26 — 10:5a: “coming into the world”; David’s words as Son’s response
**Locus:** 3356–3358

### C27 — Text of Ps 40 in Hebrews: “body” prepared; other adaptations
**Locus:** 3360–3364  
**Quote:** "First, Hebrews uses the word \"body\" instead of \"ears\" in Ps 40:6: \"a body you have prepared for me\" instead of \"ears you have prepared for me\" … It is more likely, however, that \"body\" represents an alternate translation of the original text. … The pastor builds his argument on this version of the text with which he and his hearers were familiar. … \"body\" allowed him to tie this obedience more readily to the incarnation and final offering of Christ's \"body\" on the cross. … The plural \"whole burnt offerings\" (v. 6) fits well with Hebrews' emphasis on the multiplicity, and thereby inability, of the old sacrifices. \"You were not pleased with\" (v. 6b) is a stronger expression of the divine displeasure than \"you did not request.\""  
**Claim:** (Cockerill) Hebrews’ Ps 40 differs from standard LXX (body not ears; plural burnt offerings; “not pleased”; reordered “to do, O God, your will” omitting “I have resolved”); “body” likely alternate Greek (synecdoche ears→body), not pastor’s invention against familiar text; enables incarnation/cross body-link; other changes likely pastoral for rhetoric and theology (multiplicity; stronger rejection; purpose-of-coming = do God’s will).
